content.text:
I submitted **factor-when-justified** with confidence 0.7, using 45 of the 60 budget.

**Phase 1: is it part-based?**
- I trained three tasks: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3.
- Then I tested L3-S1-M2, which only combines rules the learner had already seen. It needed 34 and 37 examples.
- A task made entirely of new rules, L4-S4-M4, needed 25 and 18. It was more similar to the trained tasks (0.56 against 0.375).
- A part-based learner should have found the recombined task cheap. It didn't, which argues against part-based.

**Phase 2: holistic or factor-when-justified?**
- I trained six more tasks so that L3, S1 and M2 each appeared in three trained tasks. That makes them parts whether k is 2 or 3. I picked these tasks so the target's highest similarity to anything trained stayed at 0.375.
- The control was L4-S3-M1. It has the same highest similarity (0.375), and each of its rules appeared in only one trained task, so none of them can be a part yet.
- Over 18 tests each:

| Task | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|
| L3-S1-M2 (rules now parts) | 17.5 |
| L4-S3-M1 (no parts) | 30.6 |

- A holistic learner should find both tasks about equally hard. A part-based learner should find both cheap, since every rule in the control had been trained. Only factor-when-justified predicts the gap I saw. The target's cost also roughly halved from phase 1 to phase 2.

**Why only 0.7:**
- The tests were very noisy: values ranged from 1 to 64, and a result of exactly 1 came up often.
- The phase 2 gap is about 2.5 standard errors, which is solid but not conclusive.
- The phase 1 evidence against part-based rests on only two samples per task.
- I didn't try to work out whether k is 2 or 3, because the verdict doesn't depend on it.
